topics: How Computers Store Text: ASCII and Unicode

data.sourceTitle: How Computers Store Text: ASCII and Unicode
data.targetTitle: How Computers Store Text: ASCII and Unicode
data.sourcePassage:
Computers can only process and store binary numbers — sequences of 0s and 1s. To store text, every character must be assigned a unique number, which is then converted to binary. The agreed mapping between characters and their numerical codes is called a character set. Without an agreed character set, a file created on one computer would appear as nonsense on another.

ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) was the original character encoding standard, developed in the 1960s. ASCII uses 7 bits per character, giving 128 possible values (2 to the power of 7 equals 128). These 128 slots cover uppercase letters A to Z, lowercase letters a to z, the digits 0 to 9, punctuation marks, spaces, and control characters such as newline and tab. Some key codes to know are: A = 65, a = 97, and the digit character '0' = 48. There is a useful pattern: uppercase and lowercase versions of the same letter always differ by exactly 32 in their ASCII values.

ASCII worked well for English text, but it had a fundamental limitation — it could only represent 128 characters, which is far too few for the world's many writing systems. Chinese alone has tens of thousands of characters, and languages such as Arabic, Hindi, and Japanese use completely different scripts that ASCII cannot represent at all. Sharing text files between countries resulted in garbled symbols wherever non-ASCII characters appeared.

Unicode was developed to solve this problem. It supports over 143,000 characters, covering virtually every written language in the world, as well as symbols and emoji. The most common implementation of Unicode is UTF-8, which uses variable-length encoding: standard ASCII characters still use just one byte (keeping UTF-8 backwards compatible with ASCII), while less common characters use two, three, or four bytes. This means UTF-8 is efficient for English text while still being able to represent any language on Earth.

topics: How Digital Images Work: Pixels and Colour

data.sourceTitle: How Digital Images Work: Pixels and Colour
data.targetTitle: How Digital Images Work: Pixels and Colour
data.sourcePassage:
A digital image is stored as a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels — short for picture elements. A pixel is the smallest addressable unit of a digital image; it cannot be divided further into any smaller meaningful part. When you zoom into a digital photograph far enough, you can see the individual coloured squares that make it up. Every image on a screen — from a simple icon to a cinema-quality film frame — is ultimately a grid of pixels.

Resolution describes the number of pixels in an image and is usually expressed as width multiplied by height. A Full HD image, for example, is 1920 by 1080 pixels, giving a total of over two million pixels. A higher resolution means more pixels and therefore more fine detail — a high-resolution photograph appears sharper and clearer than a low-resolution one of the same subject. However, more pixels also means more data to store.

Colour depth, also called bit depth, is the number of bits used to represent the colour of a single pixel. The number of possible colours is calculated using the formula 2 to the power of the colour depth. A 1-bit image can show only two colours (typically black and white). An 8-bit image can show 256 different colours. A 24-bit image uses 8 bits each for the red, green, and blue channels — giving 256 levels per channel and a total of 256 × 256 × 256 = approximately 16.7 million different colours. This is known as true colour, and it is the standard used for digital photographs.

Both resolution and colour depth affect the quality of an image. Higher resolution captures more detail; greater colour depth produces more realistic, subtly shaded colours. However, both also increase the amount of data in the image file. This creates a fundamental trade-off: higher quality always means a larger file size. In practice, compression techniques are used to reduce file sizes while preserving as much quality as possible.

data.sourcePassage:
Knowing how to calculate the file size of an uncompressed digital image is an important skill in computing. The calculation follows directly from the two properties of an image you have already studied: its resolution (the number of pixels) and its colour depth (the number of bits per pixel). The formula is straightforward: multiply the width in pixels by the height in pixels by the colour depth in bits per pixel. This gives the total number of bits in the image. To convert to bytes, divide by eight, since there are eight bits in every byte.

As a worked example, consider a small image that is 100 pixels wide and 200 pixels tall, with a colour depth of 8 bits per pixel. The calculation runs: 100 × 200 = 20,000 pixels in total; 20,000 × 8 = 160,000 bits; 160,000 ÷ 8 = 20,000 bytes, which is approximately 19.5 kilobytes. Now consider a larger photograph at 800 pixels wide and 600 pixels tall, stored in true colour at 24 bits per pixel. The calculation gives: 800 × 600 × 24 = 11,520,000 bits; divided by 8 gives 1,440,000 bytes, or approximately 1.37 megabytes. A Full HD image at 1920 by 1080 pixels in 24-bit colour would be approximately 5.93 megabytes uncompressed.

These calculations reveal something important: colour depth has a powerful effect on file size. Doubling the colour depth from 8-bit to 16-bit doubles the file size for any given image, just as doubling either the width or height doubles it. This means an image with high resolution but low colour depth can end up smaller than an image with lower resolution but higher colour depth — the result can be counterintuitive.

In practice, image files are almost always compressed before being stored or transmitted. Common formats such as JPEG use lossy compression, which discards some image data to achieve much smaller file sizes, while PNG uses lossless compression, which reduces file size without losing any data. The uncompressed calculation gives the maximum possible file size — the starting point before compression is applied.
